title: Sensitivity analysis
text:
We use two sensitivity analyses to examine whether specific data-inclusion decisions influence the overall lnRR estimate. First, we exclude the four Abramova-laboratory studies together. Second, we exclude the effect sizes that required exact-zero boundary corrections.






NoteVariable definitions










Variable
Definition




study_id
Identifier for the primary research paper.


es_id
Unique identifier for each effect size.


ex_id, con_id
Identifiers for the exposed and control groups used to construct V.


lnRR
Log response ratio for the difference in group means.


lnRR_var
Sampling variance of lnRR.


c_mean_continuity_corrected
Indicates that the control-group mean required a boundary correction.


c_sd_continuity_corrected
Indicates that the control-group SD required a boundary correction.


\(k\)
Number of effect sizes included in a model.






Analysis data and model functions
We load the effect-size database created in the Effect size calculation. The model functions reconstruct V with the variables and working correlation used in the Sampling variance-covariance matrices. Then, we fit the random-effects structure specified in the Overall effects.

# Load the complete lnRR effect-size database.
db <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "db_effect_sizes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Construct the lnRR sampling variance-covariance matrix for any subset.
construct_lnRR_vcv <- function(data) {
  metafor::vcalc(
    vi = lnRR_var,
    cluster = study_id,
    grp1 = ex_id,
    grp2 = con_id,
    w1 = ex_n,
    w2 = c_n,
    obs = es_id,
    rho = 0.5,
    checkpd = TRUE,
    data = data
  )
}

# Reconstruct V and fit the intercept-only lnRR model for any subset.
fit_lnRR_model <- function(data) {
  V <- construct_lnRR_vcv(data)

  metafor::rma.mv(
    yi = lnRR,
    V = V,
    random = list(
      ~ 1 | study_id,
      ~ 1 | es_id,
      ~ 1 | strain
    ),
    test = "t",
    method = "REML",
    sparse = TRUE,
    data = data
  )
}

# Fit the overall lnRR model before applying either exclusion.
model_all <- fit_lnRR_model(db)

# Identify the Abramova-laboratory studies and count their current effect sizes.
abramova_studies <- db |>
  dplyr::filter(grepl("^abramova_", study_id)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(study_id) |>
  dplyr::pull(study_id)

abramova_effect_sizes <- sum(db$study_id %in% abramova_studies)



Combined Abramova-laboratory exclusion
The 4 Abramova-laboratory studies contribute 98 of the 187 effect sizes. When studies from one laboratory contribute a large proportion of the data, laboratory-specific methods, experimental conditions, or reporting practices may have a disproportionate influence on the overall estimate. To examine this possibility, we remove all four studies together, reconstruct V, and compare the refitted model with the model that includes all studies.

# Remove all studies with the Abramova study identifier.
db_without_abramova <- db |>
  dplyr::filter(!study_id %in% abramova_studies)

# Reconstruct V and refit the lnRR model after the combined exclusion.
model_without_abramova <- fit_lnRR_model(db_without_abramova)

We use the same lnRR scale in both panels. Panel A shows the original overall-effect model, and Panel B shows the model after excluding the four Abramova-laboratory studies.

# Set one effect-size range for both orchard plots.
shared_effect_limits <- range(
  c(
    db$lnRR,
    model_all$pi.lb,
    model_all$pi.ub,
    model_without_abramova$pi.lb,
    model_without_abramova$pi.ub
  ),
  finite = TRUE
)
effect_padding <- diff(shared_effect_limits) * 0.05
shared_effect_limits <- shared_effect_limits + c(
  -effect_padding,
  effect_padding
)
shared_effect_breaks <- pretty(shared_effect_limits, n = 5)

# Draw the overall model that includes all studies.
plot_all <- orchaRd::orchard_plot(
  model_all,
  group = "study_id",
  xlab = "lnRR",
  flip = TRUE
) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = "Overall effect") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    limits = shared_effect_limits,
    breaks = shared_effect_breaks
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "All studies")

# Draw the model after excluding the Abramova-laboratory studies.
plot_without_abramova <- orchaRd::orchard_plot(
  model_without_abramova,
  group = "study_id",
  xlab = "lnRR",
  flip = TRUE
) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_discrete(labels = "Overall effect") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(
    limits = shared_effect_limits,
    breaks = shared_effect_breaks
  ) +
  ggplot2::labs(title = "Abramova-laboratory studies excluded")

# Place the original and sensitivity models side by side.
abramova_comparison_plot <-
  (plot_all + plot_without_abramova) +
  patchwork::plot_layout(guides = "collect") +
  patchwork::plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A") &
  ggplot2::theme(legend.position = "top")

Exact-zero effect-size exclusion
Two effect sizes required a boundary correction because the reported control-group summary statistics produced an exact-zero mean and SD. We identify these effect sizes, remove them, reconstruct V, and refit the multilevel intercept-only model.

# Identify rows that received both control-group boundary corrections.
exact_zero_ids <- db |>
  dplyr::filter(
    c_mean_continuity_corrected,
    c_sd_continuity_corrected
  ) |>
  dplyr::pull(es_id)

if (length(exact_zero_ids) == 0) {
  stop("No exact-zero-corrected effect sizes were identified.")
}

# Retain all other effect sizes for the sensitivity model.
db_without_exact_zero <- db |>
  dplyr::filter(!es_id %in% exact_zero_ids)

# Reconstruct V and refit the model after excluding the corrected rows.
model_without_exact_zero <- fit_lnRR_model(db_without_exact_zero)

We report the identifiers of the excluded effect sizes and compare the overall lnRR estimates before and after the exclusion.

# List the effect sizes removed from the sensitivity model.
tibble::tibble(`Effect size excluded` = exact_zero_ids) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Effect sizes excluded from the sensitivity model.")

title: Uni-moderators
text:
We fit one uni-moderator multilevel meta-regression for each study characteristic and effect-size type. The models use lnRR, lnVR, or lnCVR as the response and the same random-effects structure as the overall-effect model: study (study_id), effect size (es_id), and strain (strain). We construct a complete VCV matrix for each effect-size type with rho = 0.5. For categorical moderators, we remove levels with fewer than five effect sizes (\(k < 5\)) and subset the corresponding rows and columns of the matching VCV matrix.
Across every lnRR plot, negative values represent less anxiety- or depression-like behaviour and positive values represent more anxiety- or depression-like behaviour. For lnVR and lnCVR, negative values represent lower variability and positive values represent greater variability in the treatment group.
We load the effect-size database from Chapter 2 and construct a complete VCV matrix for lnRR, lnVR, and lnCVR using the same group identifiers as Chapter 3. The lnVR and lnCVR datasets exclude percentage outcomes because their effect-size values are missing by design.
# Load the effect-size database created in Chapter 2.
db <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "db_effect_sizes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# List the variables required to construct V and fit the models.
required_columns <- c(
  "study_id", "es_id", "ex_id", "con_id", "strain",
  "ex_n", "c_n",
  "lnRR", "lnRR_var", "lnVR", "lnVR_var", "lnCVR", "lnCVR_var"
)

# Stop if any required variable is missing.
if (length(setdiff(required_columns, names(db))) > 0) {
  stop("The effect-size database does not contain all model variables.")
}

# Confirm that each row has a unique effect-size identifier.
if (anyDuplicated(db$es_id)) {
  stop("es_id must identify one effect-size row.")
}

# Link each effect-size column to its sampling variance and display label.
effect_specs <- tribble(
  ~effect, ~variance, ~label, ~axis_label,
  "lnRR",  "lnRR_var",  "lnRR",  "lnRR",
  "lnVR",  "lnVR_var",  "lnVR",  "lnVR",
  "lnCVR", "lnCVR_var", "lnCVR", "lnCVR"
)

construct_metric_data <- function(data, effect, variance, rho = 0.5) {
  # Retain only rows available for this effect-size type.
  idx <- which(is.finite(data[[effect]]) & is.finite(data[[variance]]))
  metric_data <- data[idx, , drop = FALSE]

  # Construct the matching complete VCV matrix.
  V <- metafor::vcalc(
    vi = metric_data[[variance]],
    cluster = metric_data$study_id,
    grp1 = metric_data$ex_id,
    grp2 = metric_data$con_id,
    w1 = metric_data$ex_n,
    w2 = metric_data$c_n,
    obs = metric_data$es_id,
    rho = rho
  )

  list(data = metric_data, V = V)
}

# Create the three analysis datasets and complete matrices.
metric_inputs <- purrr::map2(
  effect_specs$effect,
  effect_specs$variance,
  ~ construct_metric_data(db, .x, .y, rho = 0.5)
)
names(metric_inputs) <- effect_specs$effect

effect_specs |>
  mutate(k = purrr::map_int(effect, ~ nrow(metric_inputs[[.x]]$data))) |>
  dplyr::select(`Effect size` = label, k) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Effect sizes available for the uni-moderator analyses.")

title: Sampling variance-covariance matrices
text:
We construct one sampling variance-covariance matrix for each effect-size type. Each matrix uses the corresponding sampling variances and the exposed- and control-group identifiers in the extraction database.
We first load the effect-size database and check the columns required to construct the matrices.
pacman::p_load(
  dplyr,
  knitr,
  metafor,
  purrr,
  readr,
  tibble,
  tidyr
)

project_root <- normalizePath("..", mustWork = TRUE)
derived_dir <- file.path(project_root, "Data", "derived")

# Load the effect-size database from Chapter 2.
vcv_data <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "db_effect_sizes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# List the variables required to construct V and its index.
required_columns <- c(
  "study_id", "es_id", "ex_id", "con_id", "out_id",
  "ex_n", "c_n",
  "lnRR", "lnRR_var", "lnVR", "lnVR_var", "lnCVR", "lnCVR_var"
)

if (length(setdiff(required_columns, names(vcv_data))) > 0) {
  stop("Required columns are missing from the effect-size database.")
}
if (anyDuplicated(vcv_data$es_id)) {
  stop("es_id must be unique before constructing V.")
}
if (anyNA(vcv_data[c("study_id", "es_id", "ex_id", "con_id")])) {
  stop("Study and group identifiers must be complete before constructing V.")
}
if (any(vcv_data$ex_n <= 0) || any(vcv_data$c_n <= 0)) {
  stop("Group sample sizes must be positive before constructing V.")
}

# Link each effect size to its sampling-variance column.
effect_specs <- tibble::tribble(
  ~effect, ~variance,
  "lnRR",  "lnRR_var",
  "lnVR",  "lnVR_var",
  "lnCVR", "lnCVR_var"
)

title: Data preparation
text:
Calculation methods

We estimate a missing mean from Q1, the median, Q3, and sample size with the Luo et al. method (Luo et al. 2018).
We estimate a missing SD from Q1, Q3, and sample size with the Wan et al. method (Wan et al. 2014).
When the source reports an SE but not an SD, we calculate SD = SE × sqrt(n).
When the source does not report an SE, we calculate SE = SD / sqrt(n).
We retain existing extracted values unchanged.

\[
\widehat{M} =
\left(0.7 + \frac{0.39}{n}\right)\frac{Q_1 + Q_3}{2}
+ \left(0.3 - \frac{0.39}{n}\right)M_d
\]
\[
\widehat{SD} =
\frac{Q_3-Q_1}
{2\Phi^{-1}\left(\frac{0.75n-0.125}{n+0.25}\right)}
\]
We define one function for each published estimator and one function that completes the mean, SD, and SE for either treatment arm. The function also records the source of every analysis value.

estimate_mean_luo <- function(q1, median, q3, n) {
  weight <- 0.7 + 0.39 / n
  weight * ((q1 + q3) / 2) + (1 - weight) * median
}

estimate_sd_wan <- function(q1, q3, n) {
  denominator <- 2 * stats::qnorm((0.75 * n - 0.125) / (n + 0.25))
  (q3 - q1) / denominator
}

complete_arm_statistics <- function(data, arm) {
  n <- data[[paste0(arm, "_n")]]
  mean_source <- data[[paste0(arm, "_mean")]]
  sd_source <- data[[paste0(arm, "_sd")]]
  se_source <- data[[paste0(arm, "_se")]]
  median <- data[[paste0(arm, "_median")]]
  q1 <- data[[paste0(arm, "_q1")]]
  q3 <- data[[paste0(arm, "_q3")]]

  mean_from_iqr <- is.na(mean_source) & complete.cases(q1, median, q3, n)
  sd_from_iqr <- is.na(sd_source) & complete.cases(q1, q3, n)
  sd_from_se <- is.na(sd_source) & !sd_from_iqr & !is.na(se_source) & !is.na(n)

  if (any(mean_from_iqr & !(q1 <= median & median <= q3))) {
    stop("Invalid Q1 <= median <= Q3 ordering in the ", arm, " arm.")
  }

  mean_analysis <- mean_source
  mean_analysis[mean_from_iqr] <- estimate_mean_luo(
    q1[mean_from_iqr], median[mean_from_iqr], q3[mean_from_iqr], n[mean_from_iqr]
  )

  sd_analysis <- sd_source
  sd_analysis[sd_from_iqr] <- estimate_sd_wan(
    q1[sd_from_iqr], q3[sd_from_iqr], n[sd_from_iqr]
  )
  sd_analysis[sd_from_se] <- se_source[sd_from_se] * sqrt(n[sd_from_se])

  se_analysis <- se_source
  se_from_sd <- is.na(se_analysis) & !is.na(sd_analysis) & !is.na(n)
  se_analysis[se_from_sd] <- sd_analysis[se_from_sd] / sqrt(n[se_from_sd])

  data[[paste0(arm, "_mean_analysis")]] <- mean_analysis
  data[[paste0(arm, "_mean_method")]] <- if_else(
    mean_from_iqr,
    "Luo et al. (2018): Q1, median, Q3, and n",
    "Extracted mean used unchanged"
  )
  data[[paste0(arm, "_sd_analysis")]] <- sd_analysis
  data[[paste0(arm, "_sd_method")]] <- case_when(
    sd_from_iqr ~ "Wan et al. (2014): Q1, Q3, and n",
    sd_from_se ~ "SD = SE * sqrt(n)",
    TRUE ~ "Extracted SD used unchanged"
  )
  data[[paste0(arm, "_se_analysis")]] <- se_analysis
  data[[paste0(arm, "_se_method")]] <- if_else(
    se_from_sd,
    "SE = SD / sqrt(n)",
    "Extracted SE used unchanged"
  )

  if (anyNA(mean_analysis) || anyNA(sd_analysis) || anyNA(se_analysis)) {
    stop("Unresolved summary statistic in the ", arm, " arm.")
  }

  data
}

We apply the functions to the control arm (c) and then to the exposed arm (ex). We summarise the calculation methods by arm and statistic.

with_statistics <- source_for_derivation |>
  complete_arm_statistics("c") |>
  complete_arm_statistics("ex")

method_counts <- bind_rows(
  with_statistics |> count(arm = "Control", statistic = "Mean", method = c_mean_method, name = "rows"),
  with_statistics |> count(arm = "Control", statistic = "SD", method = c_sd_method, name = "rows"),
  with_statistics |> count(arm = "Control", statistic = "SE", method = c_se_method, name = "rows"),
  with_statistics |> count(arm = "Exposed", statistic = "Mean", method = ex_mean_method, name = "rows"),

title: Prenatal chronic noise exposure meta-analysis
Effect size calculation
text:
We load the analysis-ready database from the preceding chapter and calculate three effect sizes: the log response ratio (lnRR), log variability ratio (lnVR), and log coefficient of variation ratio (lnCVR). We also calculate the sampling variance of each effect size.
pacman::p_load(
  dplyr,
  ggplot2,
  knitr,
  metafor,
  readr,
  tibble,
  tidyr
)

project_root <- normalizePath("..", mustWork = TRUE)
derived_dir <- file.path(project_root, "Data", "derived")

# Load the analysis-ready database.
db <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "PCN_analysis_ready.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

title: Effect size calculation
text:
Data types

We calculate lnRR for every outcome. We apply an arcsine-square-root transformation before calculating lnRR for percentage outcomes.
We calculate lnVR and lnCVR only for non-percentage outcomes. We exclude percentage outcomes because their bounded scale creates a mechanical relationship between the mean and variance.

title: Effect size calculation
text:
Boundary corrections

For non-percentage outcomes, we replace a zero mean with 0.9 times the smallest positive mean in the same outcome stratum.
For all outcomes, we replace a zero SD with the smallest positive SD for the same treatment arm and outcome stratum.
For percentage outcomes, we replace means of 0 and 100 with 0.5 and 99.5, respectively.

We define an outcome stratum with assay_type, measurement_variable, data_type, and data_units.

title: Effect size calculation
text:
Comparison structure

For independent comparisons, we use ROM, VR, and CVR in metafor::escalc().
For dependent comparisons, we use ROMC, VRC, and CVRC with a within-subject correlation of 0.5.

Because studies can contribute multiple dependent outcomes, we use metafor::rma.mv() with the sampling variance-covariance matrices constructed in the preceding chapter.

title: Publication bias
text:
We evaluate small-study effects and time-lag patterns for lnRR. We use the same sampling variance-covariance matrix and random-effects structure as the overall-effect model.






NoteVariable definitions










Variable
Definition




sqrt_inv_e_n
Square root of the inverse effective sample size, calculated as \(\sqrt{1/n_{ex} + 1/n_c}\).


publication_year
Publication year extracted from study_id.


year_c
Publication year centred on the mean publication year.






Analysis data and overall model
We load the effect-size database and reconstruct the complete VCV matrix with the same metafor::vcalc() specification used in Chapter 3. We then fit the intercept-only model that provides the centre line for the funnel plot.

# Load the lnRR effect sizes and sampling variances.
db <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "db_effect_sizes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Extract the four-digit publication year from study_id.
db <- db |>
  mutate(
    publication_year = as.integer(
      stringr::str_extract(study_id, "(19|20)[0-9]{2}")
    )
  )

if (anyNA(db$publication_year)) {
  stop("A publication year could not be extracted from study_id.")
}

# Construct the complete sampling VCV matrix.
VCV_lnRR <- metafor::vcalc(
  vi = lnRR_var,
  cluster = study_id,
  grp1 = ex_id,
  grp2 = con_id,
  w1 = ex_n,
  w2 = c_n,
  obs = es_id,
  rho = 0.5,
  data = db
)

# Fit the intercept-only multilevel model.
ma_all <- metafor::rma.mv(
  yi = lnRR,
  V = VCV_lnRR,
  random = list(
    ~ 1 | study_id,
    ~ 1 | es_id,
    ~ 1 | strain
  ),
  test = "t",
  method = "REML",
  sparse = TRUE,
  data = db
)

Visual inspection: funnel plot
We plot lnRR against inverse standard error. Greater values on the vertical axis represent greater precision. Negative lnRR values represent less anxiety- or depression-like behaviour, and positive values represent more.

# Draw the inverse-SE funnel plot.
metafor::funnel(
  ma_all,
  yaxis = "seinv",
  las = 1,
  digits = c(2, 1),
  xlab = "Standardised residual lnRR (- less, + more anxiety/depression-like behaviour)",
  ylab = "Precision (inverse of SE)",
  pch = 21,
  bg = scales::alpha("black", 0.2),
  col = "black",
  cex = 1.2
)










Egger-type regression
We test small-study effects with an N-based precision term. This avoids using the sampling standard error as the predictor because lnRR and its sampling variance are mathematically related (Nakagawa et al. 2022).

# Calculate the N-based precision term for every effect size.
dt_egger_full <- db |>
  mutate(
    sqrt_inv_e_n = sqrt((1 / ex_n) + (1 / c_n))
  )

# Fit the Egger-type multilevel meta-regression.
egger_model_full <- metafor::rma.mv(
  yi = lnRR,
  V = VCV_lnRR,
  mods = ~ 1 + sqrt_inv_e_n,
  random = list(
    ~ 1 | study_id,
    ~ 1 | es_id,
    ~ 1 | strain
  ),
  test = "t",
  method = "REML",
  sparse = TRUE,
  data = dt_egger_full
)

Time-lag pattern
We use publication year to test whether lnRR estimates change systematically over time. This analysis evaluates a time-lag or decline pattern, in which effect-size estimates differ between earlier and later publications. We include the N-based precision term in the same model so we can estimate the publication-year coefficient while accounting for differences in effective sample size. We centre publication year on its mean so the model intercept represents the expected lnRR at the average publication year. The model retains the same VCV matrix and random-effects structure.

    ~ 1 | es_id,

title: Leave-one-out analysis
text:
We use a leave-one-out analysis to examine whether the overall lnRR estimate depends on any single study. We remove one study at a time, reconstruct the sampling variance-covariance matrix (V), and refit the multilevel intercept-only model.






NoteVariable definitions










Variable
Definition




study_id
Identifier for the primary research paper and the unit removed in each leave-one-out iteration.


es_id
Unique identifier for each effect size.


ex_id, con_id
Identifiers for the exposed and control groups used to construct V.


lnRR
Log response ratio for the difference in group means.


lnRR_var
Sampling variance of lnRR.


\(k\)
Number of effect sizes included in a model.






Analysis data and model functions
We load the effect-size database created in the Effect size calculation. The model functions reconstruct V with the variables and working correlation used in the Sampling variance-covariance matrices. Then, we fit the random-effects structure specified in the Overall effects.

# Load the lnRR effect sizes and sampling variances.
db <- readr::read_csv(
  file.path(derived_dir, "db_effect_sizes.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

# Construct the lnRR sampling variance-covariance matrix for any subset.
construct_lnRR_vcv <- function(data) {
  metafor::vcalc(
    vi = lnRR_var,
    cluster = study_id,
    grp1 = ex_id,
    grp2 = con_id,
    w1 = ex_n,
    w2 = c_n,
    obs = es_id,
    rho = 0.5,
    checkpd = TRUE,
    data = data
  )
}

# Reconstruct V and fit the intercept-only lnRR model for any subset.
fit_lnRR_model <- function(data) {
  V <- construct_lnRR_vcv(data)

  metafor::rma.mv(
    yi = lnRR,
    V = V,
    random = list(
      ~ 1 | study_id,
      ~ 1 | es_id,
      ~ 1 | strain
    ),
    test = "t",
    method = "REML",
    sparse = TRUE,
    data = data
  )
}

# Fit the overall model before applying any exclusions.
overall_lnRR_model <- fit_lnRR_model(db)



Study-level leave-one-out analysis
Each iteration removes every effect size from one study_id. Because the number and arrangement of dependent effect sizes change after each exclusion, we reconstruct V before fitting that iteration’s model.

# Fit one model for each omitted study.
study_ids <- unique(db$study_id)

loo_models <- purrr::map(
  study_ids,
  ~ fit_lnRR_model(dplyr::filter(db, study_id != .x))
)
names(loo_models) <- study_ids

# Extract the estimate and intervals returned by each fitted model.
loo_model_results <- purrr::imap(
  loo_models,
  function(model, omitted_study) {
    result <- orchaRd::mod_results(model, group = "study_id")
    model_table <- result$mod_table
    model_data <- result$data
    model_table$name <- omitted_study
    model_data$moderator <- omitted_study
    list(mod_table = model_table, data = model_data)
  }
)

# Assemble the object used by the leave-one-out orchard plot.
loo_results <- structure(
  list(
    mod_table = dplyr::bind_rows(
      purrr::map(loo_model_results, "mod_table")
    ),
    data = dplyr::bind_rows(
      purrr::map(loo_model_results, "data")
    ),
    orig_mod_results = orchaRd::mod_results(
      overall_lnRR_model,
      group = "study_id"
    )
  ),
  class = c("orchard", "data.frame")
)

# Create a compact table with one row for each omitted study.
loo_table <- loo_results$mod_table |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Study removed` = as.character(name),
    k = nrow(db) - as.integer(table(db$study_id)[as.character(name)]),
    `Estimate` = estimate,
    `95% CI lower` = lowerCL,
    `95% CI upper` = upperCL
  )

loo_table |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Overall lnRR after removing each study in turn."
  )
